solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Old women — grey and back together among poetry lovers

parts.note: GR is a standard abbreviation for grey
taken as written

indicators.note: going back means the word is read from its end to its start

parts.note: sam is a Spenserian word for together, known only to readers of old poetry

explanation.surface: A gathering of grey-haired old ladies reunited at a poetry society.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Among poetry lovers' flags SAM as a poetic word (Spenser used it); turned round it closes GRANDMAS.
explanation.definitionFit: Grandmothers are typically older ladies, so the plural is a loose synonym for elderly females.

clue.text: Bet is fair bunkum

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to gamble, a slang verb
second meaning: a fair or cheap place of entertainment, in slang

explanation.surface: A wager declared to be fair is dismissed as rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: A triple definition: the one short slang word covers gambling, a fairground and nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: Chambers lists the slang word as a verb meaning gamble, a noun for a fair, and a noun for humbug.

clue.text: Supply ordered again — missing silver's arranged once more

indicators.note: read as the adverb of supple, these words are bent flexibly into a new order
something missing is absent, so those letters are taken out

parts.note: taken as written
Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

explanation.surface: A shop's stock is reordered, but the silver is missing from the new arrangement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supply' looks like a noun about stock; it is the adverb from supple. Remove AG from ORDERED AGAIN and rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: To ordain is to decree or arrange, so doing it again is to arrange anew.

clue.text: Rising tide covering special areas of basilicas

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means reading from bottom to top
to cover something here is to wrap around it on both sides

parts.note: the tide is a poetic term for the sea
SP is an abbreviation of special

explanation.surface: Floodwater climbing into special parts of great churches.
explanation.walkthrough: SE(SP)A is built first and then read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: An apse is the vaulted semicircular recess at the end of a church, typical of basilicas.

clue.text: Merchant's department on the point of cut and thrust?

parts.note: D is an abbreviation for department

parts.words: the point of cut and thrust?
parts.note: a slender pointed sword used for thrusting

explanation.surface: A store's department poised on the edge of a fierce commercial fight.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry D sits on top of RAPIER. Cut and thrust suggests business rivalry, but here it is swordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Drapier is an old form of draper, a cloth merchant, famous from Swift's Drapier's Letters.

clue.text: Upcoming opportunity to grab time for career

indicators.note: in a down entry, coming up means read from bottom to top
grabbing something means holding it inside

parts.note: room, as in room for manoeuvre, is scope or opportunity
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A career opportunity is coming up; seize the moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Career' looks like a job; it is the verb meaning to rush along.
explanation.definitionFit: To motor is to drive along fast, matching career as a verb of speeding.

clue.text: Inform of apparent source

parts.note: app. is an abbreviation for apparent
a river's rise is its source

explanation.surface: Telling someone where something seems to have come from.
explanation.definitionFit: To apprise someone is to notify or tell them of something.

clue.text: Admirable senior officer in short order accepted nothing

indicators.note: something accepted is taken in, so the officer holds the next letter

parts.note: Col. is the short form of colonel
O looks like zero

explanation.surface: A distinguished colonel who quickly took on nothing at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In short order' sounds like 'quickly'; it tells you the officer is abbreviated.
explanation.definitionFit: Cool is informal praise, meaning excellent or impressive.

clue.text: Lag with manners agrees

parts.note: an old lag is a convict, a con
manner in the archaic sense of kind or type

explanation.surface: A prisoner with good manners goes along with everything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lag' looks like a verb about falling behind; it is slang for a convict.
explanation.definitionFit: To consort with is to accord or be in harmony with, an older sense of agree.

clue.text: Submits ordinary term for addressing many Turks

parts.note: O is an abbreviation for ordinary
bey is a Turkish title of respect, here plural

explanation.surface: Someone yields, using the ordinary form of address for Turkish dignitaries.
explanation.definitionFit: To obey is to comply or yield to authority, so it matches submits.

clue.text: Bounty is before the wind, heading 157 degrees or so

parts.note: sailing large is sailing with the wind astern or abaft the beam
south-south-east is 157.5 degrees on the compass

explanation.surface: HMS Bounty runs before the wind on a south-easterly course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bounty' suggests the famous ship, matching the sailing surface, but it means generosity.
explanation.definitionFit: Largesse is generous giving, so it is a synonym of bounty in the sense of liberality.

clue.text: Irrational fear of happy boor I unsettled

indicators.note: anything unsettled is thrown out of its fixed order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An irrational dread of a cheerful lout who has rattled me.
explanation.definitionFit: Pyrophobia is a phobia, an irrational terror, specifically of fire.

clue.text: Depression is behind Oddfellow regressing

indicators.note: regressing means going backwards, so the letters run right to left

parts.note: American slang for the backside
OF is the abbreviation for a member of the Oddfellows friendly society

explanation.surface: A friendly-society member slipping back into low spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Depression' looks like gloom; it is a hollow in anatomy.
explanation.definitionFit: A fossa is an anatomical pit or hollow, i.e. a depression in a bone or surface.

clue.text: Approach, as before, article with attention

parts.note: the indefinite article
to give ear is to pay attention

explanation.surface: Coming closer, as earlier, with a careful piece of writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As before' marks the definition as an archaic word.
explanation.definitionFit: Anear is an obsolete verb meaning to come near to, i.e. draw close.

clue.text: Screen tart performing here?

indicators.note: performing suggests the letters putting on an act in a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Where you might show a film of a floozy on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and a description of the venue.
explanation.definitionFit: An arts centre is a community venue for films and theatre, where a performance could be screened.

clue.text: Worry about upsetting guy's trading area

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one word goes round the other

parts.note: to fret is to worry

indicators.note: to upset is to overturn, so the word is turned backwards

parts.note: a guy is a rope steadying a tent or mast

explanation.surface: Anxiety over a man upsetting things at a business district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guy' looks like a man; it is a guy rope.
explanation.definitionFit: A free port is a port or zone where goods are traded without customs duties.

clue.text: Pole in favour of last of these nuts

parts.note: to be for something is to favour it

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter only

parts.note: final letter of the word
mast is the fallen nuts of beech and oak

explanation.surface: A Polish supporter of the last of these nuts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pole' tempts as a nationality; it is a spar on a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: The foremast is the mast nearest a ship's bow, a vertical spar.

clue.text: Scots rail at hiding each British slight inconvenience

indicators.note: to hide something is to keep it out of sight inside

parts.note: flite is Scots for to scold
ea. is the abbreviation for each
B is the abbreviation for British

explanation.surface: Scots complaining at the British over a minor nuisance.
explanation.definitionFit: A fleabite is a trifling annoyance, figuratively something as small as an insect's nip.

clue.text: Witty reply is somewhat indecent about nearly all being topless

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: ripe humour is risqué

indicators.note: without a top means the first letter is cut off

parts.note: most is nearly all

explanation.surface: A risqué comeback about almost everyone going topless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Somewhat indecent' sounds like a mild description of the scene; ripe is the term for bawdy humour.
explanation.definitionFit: A riposte is a quick retort, originally a fencing counter-thrust.

clue.text: Having no blade? Therefore back retaining early payment

indicators.note: to retain is to hold within
back means the word reads from end to start

parts.note: so means therefore
arles is earnest money paid to seal a bargain or hiring

explanation.surface: Bladeless, so paid back with an advance.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the blade belongs to an oar, not a knife.
explanation.definitionFit: A boat without oars lacks the flat paddles, the blades, used to row.

clue.text: Cover female put on adult article

parts.note: the female pronoun
A is a film rating for adult
the definite article

explanation.surface: A woman dressing a grown-up in a garment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put on' reads as dressing; in a down entry it means placed above.
explanation.definitionFit: To sheathe is to encase in a protective covering, as a sword in its scabbard.

clue.text: Fourth estate stuff

definitions.meaning: first meaning: journalists and newspapers collectively
second meaning: to cram or push down tightly

explanation.walkthrough: The fourth estate is the traditional name for the news media, after the three estates of the realm.
explanation.definitionFit: Journalism is collectively called by this word, and to cram or squeeze something is to do the same verb.

clue.text: Eg, Welsh plod put up evidence to detain licentiate

parts.note: PC Plod is slang for a police constable

indicators.note: in a down entry, putting up means reading upwards
to detain is to hold inside

parts.note: to cite is to adduce as evidence
L is the abbreviation for licentiate

explanation.surface: A Welsh bobby producing evidence to hold a licensed professional.
explanation.walkthrough: P-Celtic is the Brythonic branch (Welsh, Cornish, Breton), as opposed to Goidelic Q-Celtic; plod is British slang for the police.
explanation.definitionFit: Welsh is an example of the Brythonic languages, the group linguists call P-Celtic.

clue.text: Commonwealth-era brigand to free old monarch

parts.note: to rid is to free
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the late queen

explanation.surface: A Cromwellian outlaw sets out to liberate a deposed king.
explanation.walkthrough: The Commonwealth here is Cromwell's 1650s republic; a rider was a Border mosstrooper of the time.
explanation.definitionFit: Chambers records rider as a mounted raider or moss-trooper of the 17th-century Borders, a kind of bandit.

clue.text: Clinic finally probing new ethics for those who suffered with TB

indicators.note: a probe goes into something, so this letter is inserted
a new version is a rearranged one

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter only

parts.note: last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A clinic investigates new ethical rules for tuberculosis patients.
explanation.definitionFit: A hectic, as a noun, is a consumptive patient, named from the hectic fever of tuberculosis.

clue.text: Stamped on document, "force unit into region"

indicators.note: going into something means being placed inside it

parts.note: an end is a district, as in the East End
F is the symbol for force
an ace is a single unit, one

explanation.surface: A document stamped with an order to send troops into a district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Force unit' reads as a military detachment; it is two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To enface is to write or print something on the face of a bill or document.

clue.text: Cruel ulcer

definitions.meaning: first meaning: fierce or wicked, an archaic adjective
second meaning: a whitlow, an infected sore on a finger

explanation.definitionFit: The word is an old adjective for savage or wicked and a noun for a whitlow, a painful sore.

clue.text: Work at old manuscript's sentences

parts.note: to do a task is to work at it
O is an abbreviation for old
MS is the abbreviation for manuscript

explanation.surface: Studying an ancient manuscript's lines of text.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sentences' looks grammatical; it means judicial judgments.
explanation.definitionFit: A doom is a judgment or penalty passed by a court, so dooms are verdicts.

clue.text: Some titbit as temptation?

indicators.note: some of the words means only part of their run of letters is wanted

parts.note: spans the end of the first word to the start of the last

explanation.surface: Offering a little morsel to tempt someone.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as the definition: a small sample offered to whet the appetite.
explanation.definitionFit: A taste is a small sample of food, the sort of mouthful given to entice.

clue.text: What's essential for porcelain to hold a good drink?

indicators.note: holding something means keeping it inside

parts.note: china clay, the key ingredient of porcelain
taken as written
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: Asking what it takes for a china cup to hold a fine drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Kaoliang is a strong Chinese spirit distilled from sorghum, so a liquor.

clue.text: Profit further losing leader

indicators.note: losing the leader means the first letter goes

parts.note: again means moreover, further

explanation.surface: Profits rise further after the boss departs.
explanation.definitionFit: Gain and profit are synonyms for money made or an advantage obtained.

clue.text: Answer lecturer in reverse of tender quip that's off the cuff

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for answer

indicators.note: the reverse of a word reads end to start
the lecturer is placed in, that is set inside, the other word rather than beside it

parts.note: a tender is a bid, an offer
L is the abbreviation for lecturer

explanation.surface: A lecturer's answer, a tender remark, delivered without notes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tender' looks like an adjective; it is a noun meaning a formal offer.
explanation.definitionFit: An ad lib is an improvised remark, spoken spontaneously without preparation.

clue.text: Critically examine a hull

parts.note: to test is to examine critically
taken as written

explanation.surface: Inspecting a ship's hull closely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hull' looks nautical; it is the outer husk of a seed.
explanation.definitionFit: A testa is the hard outer coat of a seed, which botanists also call its hull.

clue.text: Phantom payment by pharmacy expressing eccentricity

parts.note: scot is an old tax or payment, as in scot-free

indicators.note: to express is to squeeze out, so a letter is pressed out of the word

parts.note: a chemist is the British word for a pharmacy
e is the mathematical symbol for eccentricity

explanation.surface: A ghostly bill from the pharmacy shows how odd it is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Expressing' looks like 'showing'; it means pressing out.
explanation.definitionFit: Scotch mist is used sarcastically for something imaginary or not really there, like a ghost.

clue.text: Temper it with female article in Le Monde?

parts.note: 't is the archaic shortened form of it
the French feminine indefinite article

explanation.surface: Moderating a piece by a woman in a French newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: Le Monde is a French daily, so the article is French; the question mark marks the example.
explanation.definitionFit: To tune an instrument is to adjust its pitch, an old sense of temper.

clue.text: As before overshadow Earl replacing one grand in the flicks?

indicators.note: replacing means one thing takes another's place

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for earl
I is one and G is a grand
the big screen is the cinema

explanation.surface: An earl overshadows a big shot at the cinema.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As before' marks an archaic word; the flicks is British slang for the cinema.
explanation.definitionFit: To bescreen is an old verb for to cover or shelter from view, i.e. cast into shadow.
